quiz.why: Wind is air moving past something. Picking 'a gas made by trees' is an old idea. Trees are moved by the wind.

quiz.p: Divya pumps up a flat football. Then she weighs it. What has changed?
quiz.why: More air has been squeezed into the ball, and air has weight. So the ball is a little heavier. Picking 'lighter' comes from thinking air makes things float.

quiz.p: When the fridge door opens, where does the cold air go?
opts: Out at the bottom and down to the floor
quiz.why: Cold air is heavier for its size, so it pours out at the bottom and sinks to the floor. Picking 'up to the ceiling' mixes it up with warm air.

quiz.p: Why does cool air slide under warm air?
opts: Cool air is denser, so it is heavier for its size
quiz.why: Cool air is denser, so a litre of it is heavier, and it sinks under the lighter warm air. Picking 'cool air is faster' mixes things up: the particles in cool air move more slowly.

quiz.p: Lakshmi lives in Puri, by the sea. Which way does the breeze usually blow in the afternoon?
opts: From the sea onto the land
From the land out to sea
There is no breeze by the sea
quiz.why: In the afternoon the land is warmer than the sea, so a sea breeze flows in from the sea. Picking 'from the land' is the night-time land breeze.

quiz.p: Why does the land breeze blow at night?
opts: The land cools faster than the sea, so the sea is warmer
quiz.why: At night the land cools down faster than the sea. Now the sea is warmer, its air rises, and the cooler land air flows out to sea.

quiz.p: What holds a kite up in the sky?
opts: Moving air pushes on its tilted face, and the string holds it
quiz.why: Moving air pushes on the kite's tilted face, and the string holds it against the wind, so the push holds it up. Picking 'it is lighter than air' is a common guess, but a kite falls when the wind stops.

quiz.p: Kiran wants to fly his kite but there is no wind. What should he do?
quiz.why: Running pulls the kite through the still air, so air moves past it and holds it up.

quiz.p: Why do all the blades of a windmill tilt the same way?
opts: So the wind pushes every blade round in the same direction
quiz.why: Tilted blades turn the wind's push into a sideways push. When all tilt the same way, every blade is pushed round in the same direction, so the wheel turns.

quiz.p: What does a wind turbine do?
opts: It uses the wind to turn a generator and make electricity
quiz.why: The wind turns its blades, and the blades turn a generator, which makes electricity. Picking 'makes wind' mixes it up with a fan.

quiz.p: Galileo thought the trade winds were air left behind by the spinning Earth. What did Halley show instead?
opts: The winds are blown by the sea
The Sun's heating drives the winds
quiz.why: Halley gathered sailors' reports into a map and argued that the Sun's heating drives the winds. Later, Hadley showed that the Earth's spin bends them.

quiz.p: A kite gets stuck on an electric wire. What should you do?
opts: Leave it and tell a grown-up
quiz.why: Never pull the string or climb to reach it. Electric wires can kill. Leave the kite and tell a grown-up.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, holds a tissue strip and walks fast across a room with the fan off. The strip streams out behind her. Why?
opts: The room had a hidden wind
She was moving through the air, so air moved past the strip
items.why: The air in the room stayed still, but Kavya moved through it, so air rushed past the strip. Wind is air moving past something, whichever one is moving. A strong answer says the strip moved through the air.

items.p: Air weighs nothing at all.
items.why: False. A litre of air weighs a little over 1 gram. The air in a bedroom weighs about as much as a grown-up child. We do not feel it because it presses on us equally from all sides.

items.p: When air is warmed, it spreads out and takes up more space. We say it ____.
items.why: Expand means spread out and take up more space. Warm air expands, so a litre of it weighs less than a litre of cool air.

items.p: Lakshmi opens the fridge and holds agarbatti smoke near the bottom shelf. Where does the smoke go?
opts: Out of the fridge and down to the floor
items.why: The cold air inside the fridge is denser than the room air, so it pours out at the bottom and sinks to the floor, carrying the smoke with it. A strong answer says the cold air is heavier.

items.p: In the fridge test, you felt the cold air on your feet first, not on your face. Explain why.
items.a: Cold air is heavier than the same amount of warm air. So when the door opened, the cold air poured out at the bottom and flowed along the floor, over my feet.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that cold air is heavier, or denser, and says that it sinks and flows low.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a wind from the sea onto the land in the daytime
a wind from the land out to sea at night
a rising column of warm air
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: It is 3 pm on a sunny day in May on the beach at Chennai. Which way is the breeze most likely to blow?
opts: From the sea onto the land
From the land out to sea
There is never wind on a beach
items.why: By afternoon the sand and land are much warmer than the sea. The warm air over the land rises, and the cooler sea air slides in under it. That is the sea breeze.

items.p: Draw a beach in the afternoon. Draw an arrow for the warm air over the land, and an arrow for the breeze. Label the land and the sea.
items.art: A blank outline of a beach with sea on the left and land on the right.
items.a: Warm air rising over the land, and an arrow along the ground from the sea onto the land.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the air going up over the warm land and the breeze flowing in low from the sea to take its place.

items.p: Farhan makes a list of things on a windy day. Sort them: is the wind moving it, or is it moving by itself?
items.a: see items
items.why: Washing, a kite, leaves and a windmill are all moved by the wind. A walking dog, a crawling ant and a car move by themselves. A circling black kite uses the rising air, but chooses where to fly. A strong answer says what is pushing each thing.

items.p: Revathi's kite will not fly on a still morning. What can she do to fly it?
opts: Run with it, so air moves past it
Fly it indoors with the windows shut
items.why: A kite needs air moving past it. Running, or walking backwards, pulls the kite through the still air, so air moves past it and pushes it up.

items.p: A wind needs something, like a fan or a mouth, to blow it.
items.why: False. Most winds have no blower. They start when one place is warmer than the next, and cooler, heavier air slides in under the warmer air. Your fridge test showed air flowing with nothing pushing it.

items.p: Two cousins in Kochi are on the beach in the afternoon, feeling the cool breeze.

views.says: The sea is blowing the wind at us. It comes from the sea, so the sea must make it.
The land is making the wind. The hot land warms the air, and the sea air comes in to fill its place.

items.ask: Which cousin do you agree with? Use something you did in this unit as evidence. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence, such as the fridge test or the soil and water test. It sees that the sea is where the breeze comes from, so Anu is right about the direction. But the cause is the warm land. Nila sees that the land starts it, because the air over the land rises and makes room.
items.why: Both cousins see part of it. The breeze comes from the sea, but it starts because the land warms up and its air rises. Evidence from the fridge test and the soil and water test helps decide.

items.p: Three of these are moved by the wind's push. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Kites, sailboats and windmills are all pushed by moving air. A ceiling fan is the other way round: it uses electricity to push the air.

items.p: Many people think 'hot air just rises by itself'. Use what you learned to explain what really pushes it up.
items.a: Warm air is lighter for its size, so the heavier, cooler air around it sinks and slides under it. That pushes the warm air up.
items.why: A strong answer says that the cooler, heavier air sinks under the warm air and pushes it up, as in the fridge test.

items.p: Put the steps of a sea breeze in order.
items: Cool air from the sea slides in under it
The land gets warmer than the sea
The Sun shines on the land and the sea
The warm air over the land rises
a: The Sun shines on the land and the sea
The land gets warmer than the sea
The warm air over the land rises
Cool air from the sea slides in under it
items.why: First the Sun shines. The land warms faster than the sea. The air over the land warms and rises. The cooler sea air flows in to take its place.

items.p: Label the picture of a kite flying: the wind, the string, the tail, and the push of the air on the kite.
items.art: An unlabelled drawing of a kite on a string in the wind, with four empty label boxes.
items.a: Wind arrow coming towards the kite's face, the string from the kite to the flyer, the tail at the bottom, and a push arrow going up and back from the kite's face.
items.why: A strong answer shows the push of the air going up and back, and the string holding the kite against the wind.

items.p: Arjun's mother opens the fridge and holds smoke near the top of the open door. It drifts gently into the fridge. Why?
opts: The fridge sucks in air with a pump
Warm air flows in at the top to replace the cold air pouring out at the bottom
The light inside pulls the smoke
items.why: Cold air is pouring out at the bottom. Warm room air flows in at the top to take its place. A strong answer links the top and the bottom: one flow out, one flow in.

items.p: Meenakshi says the fridge test proves that cold air is heavier. Her brother says it only proves that cold air comes out of fridges. What would you add to the test to convince her brother?
items.a: I would try the same thing somewhere else with cold air, such as a tumbler full of ice. If smoke sinks next to the ice and rises next to a hot tumbler, then cold air sinks everywhere, not only in fridges.
items.why: A strong answer suggests a new test with cold and warm air that has nothing to do with fridges.

items.p: In Soil or Water, the soil got warmer in the sun. Then both bowls went into the shade. What usually happens?
opts: Both cool at exactly the same speed
items.why: Soil warms quickly and also cools quickly. Water warms and cools slowly. That is why, at night, the land becomes cooler than the sea, and the land breeze blows.

items.p: At night on a coast, the land is cooler than the sea, so the wind blows from the land to the sea. This is called a ____ breeze.
items.why: A land breeze blows from the land to the sea at night, because the land cools faster than the sea.

items.p: Three people in Visakhapatnam talk about wind turbines.

views.says: We should build more wind turbines. Wind is free, and turbines make electricity without smoke.
The turbines on our land pay us rent, but they only make electricity when the wind blows.
Some birds and bats are killed when they fly into the blades. We must think about where we put turbines.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing each of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer weighs real trade-offs: wind gives clean electricity without smoke, but turbines need the right windy places, cost a lot to build, and can harm birds that fly into them. It gives each person something they have right.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Wind power is clean, but it depends on the wind, costs money to build, and must be placed with care for birds.

items.p: In the Windmill That Lifts, the clip took 15 seconds at 50 cm from the fan and 45 seconds at 150 cm. What does this show?
opts: Faster wind makes the windmill work faster
The clip is heavier far from the fan
Distance has nothing to do with it
The fan is weaker on the left
items.why: Near the fan the wind was faster, and the windmill did the same job in a third of the time. Faster wind pushes much harder, so the blades turn faster.

items.p: A black kite circling high up without flapping is being held up by rising warm air.
items.why: True. A black kite must search a big area for food, and flapping uses a lot of energy. By circling in a thermal, a column of rising warm air, the bird rises without flapping and saves energy.

items.p: Draw a windmill's blades from the front. Draw an arrow to show which way they will turn when the wind blows at them.
items.art: A blank circle for the windmill's centre.
items.a: Four or more blades, all tilted the same way, with a curved arrow going round.
items.why: A strong drawing shows all the blades tilted the same way, so the wind pushes each one round in the same direction.

items.p: Selvi wants to fly her patang from her building. Which place is safest?
opts: The edge of a roof with no railing
The road in front of the building
An open terrace with a railing, away from electric wires
Next to the electric pole, where it is windy
items.why: A terrace with a railing, away from wires, is safest. Never fly a kite near electric wires, from a roof edge, or on a road.

items.p: Kite string coated with glass, called manja, cuts other kites. Explain one problem it causes for birds, and what kite flyers can do instead.
items.a: Birds fly into the thread and are badly cut, and many die. Kite flyers can use plain cotton thread, which does not cut birds.
items.why: A strong answer starts with the bird's problem: they cannot see the thin thread and fly into it. Then it gives a fix, such as plain cotton thread.

items.p: Sort these winds. Is each one mainly caused by warm and cool places, or by something pushing the air?
cats: Warm place next to a cool place
items: Warm place next to a cool place
Warm place next to a cool place
Warm place next to a cool place
cold air from an open fridge
Warm place next to a cool place
items.a: see items
items.why: The sea breeze, land breeze, monsoon and the fridge air all come from a warm place next to a cool one. A ceiling fan, a hand fan and a blown balloon push the air.

items.p: Bengaluru is far from the sea. Will a sea breeze reach it every afternoon?
opts: No, it is too far from the sea
items.why: A sea breeze travels many kilometres inland, but not hundreds. Bengaluru is about 300 kilometres from the nearest sea, too far. Its breezes have other causes.

items.p: Label the picture of the Breeze in a Box: the warm side, the cool side, and the arrows that show which way the smoke flowed.
items.art: A side view of a box with a tumbler at each end and empty label boxes.
items.a: Hot tumbler labelled warm, ice tumbler labelled cool, an arrow along the bottom from the ice to the hot cup, and an arrow up over the hot cup.
items.why: A strong answer shows the cool air flowing low towards the warm side and rising there, like a sea breeze.

items.p: Three of these are signs that you can see the wind's push. Which is the odd one out?
opts: A shadow moving across the floor during the day
items.why: Flapping washing, a turning windmill and a bending coconut tree all show moving air pushing. A shadow moves because the Sun moves across the sky, not because of the wind.

items.p: Match each living being to how they use the wind.
pairs: rises on thermals to search for food without flapping
sends seeds with silky hairs away on the breeze
lets the wind carry pollen to other maize plants
floats on a silk thread to a new place
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one uses moving air to solve a problem in their life: finding food over a wide area, sending seeds away from the parent, or carrying pollen.

items.p: Riya says, 'A kite flies because it is lighter than air.' Is she right? Explain.
items.a: No. A kite is heavier than air. It flies because moving air pushes on its tilted face, and the string holds it against the wind, so the push holds it up.
items.why: A strong answer says that the kite is held up by the push of moving air, not by being lighter. If the wind stops, the kite falls.

items.p: Imagine the fridge was full of hot air instead of cold air, like an oven that has just been switched off. Predict what smoke would do at the bottom and the top of the open door. Explain.
items.a: At the top, the hot air would pour out and rise, so the smoke would flow out and up. At the bottom, cooler room air would flow in, so the smoke would go in.
items.why: A strong answer turns the fridge result upside down, because hot air is lighter and rises. Never test this near a hot oven without a grown-up.

items.p: Galileo thought the trade winds blow from the east because the spinning Earth leaves the air behind. Which fact shows that the spin cannot be the main cause?
opts: The Earth spins towards the east
The monsoon winds turn round with the seasons, but the Earth spins the same way all year
items.why: The Earth spins the same way all year. But the monsoon winds near India change direction with the seasons. Something that changes with the seasons, the Sun's heating, must be driving them.

items.p: Two scientists explain the monsoon.

views.says: The monsoon is a giant sea breeze. The land of Asia gets hotter than the ocean in summer, so the ocean air flows in.

views.who: Sulochana Gadgil, Indian Institute of Science
views.says: The monsoon comes with a belt of rising air and rain clouds that moves north with the Sun. That is why the rains can stop for weeks in the middle of the season.

items.ask: Which picture do you find more convincing? Say why. Then say what the other picture explains well.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both use the Sun's uneven heating. Halley's picture explains why the wind comes from the sea in summer. Gadgil's picture explains things the simple one cannot, such as the breaks in the rains. A good answer says what evidence would help decide.
items.why: Scientists still discuss this. Both views agree the Sun's uneven heating drives the monsoon. They differ on the best picture of how.

items.p: A room has a window near the floor and a ventilator near the ceiling. On a hot day, how will air flow through the room?
opts: In at the low window, out at the high ventilator
In at the high ventilator, out at the low window
It will not move at all
Only in at both, never out
items.why: The warm air in the room rises and goes out of the high ventilator. Cooler air from outside comes in at the low window to take its place, as in the fridge test turned round.

items.p: In a space station there is no gravity pulling things down. A candle flame there is round, and warm air does not rise. Use this to explain what really makes warm air rise on Earth.
items.a: On Earth, gravity pulls the heavier cool air down more strongly than the light warm air. So the cool air sinks underneath and pushes the warm air up. With no gravity, nothing is heavier, so nothing sinks and nothing rises.
items.why: A strong answer says that rising needs the heavier air to sink, and sinking needs gravity.

items.p: Draw the path of the air in a full sea breeze loop: along the ground, up, high in the sky, and down again. Label where it is warm and where it is cool.
items.art: A blank outline of a coast with sea and land, and lots of sky above.
items.a: A loop: low from sea to land, up over the warm land, back out over the sea high up, and down over the cool sea.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a closed loop, because the air that rises over the land has to go somewhere, and the air that slid in from the sea has to be replaced.

items.p: A wind twice as fast pushes about four times as hard. A breeze pushes on a wall with a force of 10 units. About how hard would a wind twice as fast push?
items.why: Twice as fast means about four times the push. 4 times 10 is 40. This is why strong winds are so much more dangerous than gentle ones.

items.p: A wind turbine makes the wind behind it a little slower.
items.why: True. The turbine takes energy from the wind to turn its blades, so the air leaving it is moving more slowly. That is why turbines in a wind farm are spaced well apart.

items.p: Lakshmamma's father sailed out with the land breeze before dawn and home with the sea breeze in the afternoon. What would happen to his plan on a cloudy, cool day? Explain.
items.a: On a cloudy day the land would not get much warmer than the sea. So the sea breeze might be weak or might not come at all, and it would be hard to sail home.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sea breeze needs the land to be warmer than the sea, and clouds stop the sun warming the land.

items.p: Farhan builds two windmills. One has 4 paper blades. One has 4 card blades twice as big. At 150 cm from the fan, which will probably lift more clips?
items.why: Bigger blades catch more wind and get a bigger push. Stiff card also keeps its tilt. So the big card blades will probably lift more. The only way to be sure is to test.

items.p: Label a wind turbine: the blades, the tower, the box with the generator inside, and the wire that carries the electricity away.
items.art: An unlabelled drawing of a wind turbine with four empty label boxes.
items.a: Three long blades at the top, a tall tower, a box behind the blades with the generator, and a wire running down to the ground.
items.why: A strong answer shows the blades turning the generator in the box.

items.p: Sort these into 'warms up fast in the sun' and 'warms up slowly'.
items.a: see items
items.why: Dry soil, sand, rock and a concrete terrace warm fast in the sun. Deep water, a pond and the sea warm slowly, because the warmth spreads deep into the water. A strong answer links fast-warming places to rising air.

items.p: A city of concrete and tar gets hotter in the day than the green fields around it. Predict which way the breeze will blow at the city's edge on a sunny afternoon, and explain.
items.a: From the fields into the city. The air over the hot city rises, and the cooler air from the fields slides in under it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the same rule as the sea breeze, for a new place: cooler air flows towards the warmer place.

items.p: Which of these does NOT need moving air?
opts: A ball rolling down a slope
items.why: Kites, sailboats and seeds with silky hairs all need moving air to travel. A ball rolling down a slope is moved by gravity, and it would roll even with no air at all.

items.p: Air flows from places where it is cooler and heavier to places where it is ____ and lighter.
items.why: Cool, dense air sinks and slides under warm, light air. So near the ground, air flows towards the warmer place.

items.p: Halley's map of 1686 was one of the first weather maps. How did he collect the information for it?
opts: From many sailors' reports of the winds, and his own voyage
items.why: Halley gathered reports from sailors who had crossed many oceans, and added what he had felt himself on a voyage to St Helena. Putting many people's observations together showed the pattern.

applications: Wind turbines make electricity, for example in the wind farms of Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.
Sailboats and kattumarams travel by the wind.
Builders place windows on opposite sides of a room so breezes cool it without a fan.
Weather forecasters predict sea breezes, monsoons and cyclones by studying where the air is warm and cool.
Farmers winnow grain in a breeze, so the light husk blows away and the heavy grain falls.
Kite festivals, such as Uttarayan in Gujarat and Sankranti in Hyderabad.

open_questions.q: How will the Indian monsoon change as the Earth gets warmer?
open_questions.why_open: Computer models do not all agree. Some show more rain in total but more dry breaks and more very heavy days. Scientists are still studying it.

open_questions.q: Why does the monsoon sometimes stop for weeks in the middle of the season?
open_questions.why_open: These 'breaks' are linked to the movement of rain belts and to the oceans, but scientists cannot yet predict them well.

open_questions.q: How do birds find thermals they cannot see?
open_questions.why_open: Birds may feel the rising air on their wings, watch other birds, or notice warm ground. How much each one matters is still being studied.

maths.problem: A 1 litre bottle of air weighs about 1 gram. A big 20 litre water can full of air holds 20 litres. About how much does that air weigh?
maths.explain: Each litre of air weighs about 1 gram. There are 20 litres. 20 groups of 1 gram is 20 grams. That is about as heavy as four 5-rupee coins.
maths.context: This is about the weight of air. Air is real stuff, and each litre weighs a little over 1 gram.
maths.why_maths: Air is too light to weigh in a bottle at home. Multiplying lets us work out how heavy a big amount of air is.

maths.problem: In the Windmill That Lifts, the clip took 15 seconds to rise at 50 cm from the fan, and 45 seconds at 150 cm. How many times as long did it take far away?
maths.explain: 45 divided by 15 is 3. So the windmill took 3 times as long far from the fan. Check: 15 + 15 + 15 = 45.
maths.context: This is about the windmill experiment. A paper windmill wound up a thread and lifted a paper clip, near a fan and far from it.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'it was slower' tells us little. Dividing tells us exactly how much slower.

maths.problem: In Soil or Water, both bowls started at 30 degrees. After 30 minutes in the sun, the soil was at 42 degrees and the water at 34 degrees. How many degrees did each one warm up? How many times as much did the soil warm?
maths.answer: The soil warmed 12 degrees and the water 4 degrees. The soil warmed 3 times as much.
maths.explain: 42 minus 30 is 12. 34 minus 30 is 4. 12 divided by 4 is 3. So the soil warmed 3 times as much as the water.
maths.context: This is about the Soil or Water experiment. A bowl of soil and a bowl of water sat in the sun for 30 minutes.
maths.why_maths: The warming is what drives a sea breeze. Subtracting the start from the end shows how much each one warmed, so we can compare them fairly.

maths.problem: Meera kept a Breeze Diary in Kochi for 5 days. The strip streamed away from the sea at 3 pm on 4 of the 5 days. On the fifth day it was cloudy and the strip hung still. If she keeps the diary for 10 sunny days, on about how many will she expect a sea breeze at 3 pm? Why?
maths.answer: On about 10 days, or nearly all of them.
maths.explain: On every sunny day she recorded, the breeze came. The only day without it was cloudy. So on sunny days she can expect a sea breeze almost every afternoon. The pattern lets her predict.
maths.context: This is about the Breeze Diary project. A child checks a tissue strip at the window three times a day for 5 days.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in many days of records lets you predict what is likely, not just describe what happened.

maths.problem: A wind twice as fast pushes about 4 times as hard. A wind three times as fast pushes about 9 times as hard. Can you spot the pattern? How hard would a wind four times as fast push?
maths.explain: 2 times 2 is 4. 3 times 3 is 9. So the pattern is the speed times itself. 4 times 4 is 16.
maths.context: This is about how the wind pushes. Faster winds push much harder than slow ones.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern explains why a cyclone, which is only a few times faster than a breeze, does so much more damage.

roots.context: We have watched cold air pour out of a fridge, felt the sea breeze in a story, and seen moving air lift kites and turn windmills. Now we ask what the wind tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: When you opened the fridge, nobody blew, yet cold air poured out over your feet. Cold air is heavier than the same amount of warm air, so it slid under the room air. The sea breeze starts the same way, as cool sea air slides in under warm land air. So a wind needs no blower, only a warm place next to a cool one.
deep_truth.habit: We speak of the wind as if something blows it, like breath from a mouth or air from a fan. But most winds have no blower. They are air flowing by itself, from where it is cooler and heavier to where it is warmer and lighter.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Open Fridge test, smoke near the floor flowed out and down as soon as the door opened, and bare feet felt the cold air first. Nothing in the fridge was pushing. When the door closed, the flow stopped.

three.who_am_i: Every breath you take is a small wind. Your chest makes room, and the air outside flows in to fill it.
three.what_is_life: A black kite, the bird, rises on warm air without a single flap. Seeds of the erukku plant travel on the breeze to find new ground.
three.what_is_this_world: The whole sky is always moving, because the Sun warms some places more than others, and the air keeps flowing to even it out.

roots.thread: If the Sun warmed every place the same, the air would rest. Because the Earth is uneven, with land and sea, hills and plains, day and night, the air never rests. From one simple rule, cooler air sliding under warmer air, come sea breezes, land breezes, monsoons and trade winds, all joined into one moving sky. The breeze at your window is part of that one sky.

teachings.teaching: In this teaching, the wind, Vayu, is called the gatherer. When a fire goes out, it goes into the wind. When the Sun sets, it goes into the wind. Within the body, the breath, prana, is the gatherer in the same way.
teachings.link: The wind really does gather. The air over the whole Earth is one body of air, and the wind carries warmth, water vapour, smoke and seeds from one place to another.

teachings.teaching: The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows. It is empty, yet it never runs out. The more it moves, the more it brings forth.
teachings.link: A bellows blows air by making room. The wind, too, flows in wherever warm air has risen and made room for it.

science.text: Winds blow because the Sun heats the Earth unevenly. The flowing air carries heat from the hot tropics towards the cold poles.
Air from one part of the world mixes all around the Earth within about a year.
Exactly how the monsoon will change as the Earth gets warmer is not yet known.

other_view.view: The wind is the movement of gas from high pressure to low pressure, and nothing more. Calling the sky one body, or comparing the wind to breath, adds a feeling to the science but does not help anyone forecast tomorrow's weather.

practice.title: Feel the small wind of your breath
practice.say: Sit comfortably and hold one hand in front of your mouth. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Now breathe out gently through your mouth onto your hand. Feel that little wind? Do it three more times. Each time you breathe in, your chest makes room, and air flows in by itself. Now sit still and listen for the wind outside.
practice.kid: Sit still. Hold your hand in front of your mouth. Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out onto your hand. Feel the little wind? Do it three times. Then listen for the wind outside.

ask: If nobody blows the wind, what is the wind doing?
The air you breathe in has been to many other places. Where might it have been before?
A kite needs wind, but it also needs a string holding it back. Can holding back help something rise?
roots.art: A child sitting on a terrace at dusk with one hand in front of their mouth, with a faint breeze lifting a kite tail and the edge of the sea far away.

playtest: Every activity was walked through for a city flat. The fridge test is the spine investigation because every family with a fridge gets the result: bare feet feel the cold air within seconds, and smoke at the bottom of the open door bends out and down. The top-of-door inflow is gentler, so the steps say so. Families with no agarbatti, or with asthma, use a tissue strip and bare feet. The door is opened for at most half a minute at a time. how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, sailors knew the trade winds, steady winds that blow from the east over the warm seas near the equator. Galileo and Kepler, in the early 1600s, thought they knew why. The Earth spins towards the east, they said, and the air cannot keep up, so it is left behind as an east wind. In 1686, the English astronomer Edmond Halley collected sailors' reports of the winds from many oceans. He had felt the trade winds himself, on a voyage to the island of St Helena. He drew them on a map, one of the first weather maps ever made, and the map included the monsoons of the seas near India. The monsoon winds turn round with the seasons, but the Earth spins the same way all year. So the Earth's spin could not be the main cause. Halley said the Sun is the cause. Air over the hottest places is warmed and rises, and cooler air flows in to take its place. In 1735, George Hadley added the last piece. The spin does not make the winds, but it bends them once they move. That is why air flowing towards the equator arrives from the east.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler, who had the first idea, Edmond Halley, an English astronomer, and George Hadley, an English lawyer and scientist
how_we_found_out.when: Early 1600s (the spin idea), 1686 (Halley's map and paper) and 1735 (Hadley's paper)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Galileo and Kepler thought the trade winds were air left behind by the spinning Earth. Halley's map showed that winds such as the monsoon change with the seasons, which the spin alone cannot do, and that the Sun's heating drives them. Hadley then showed that the spin is still part of the story: it bends the winds as they flow.
